apush-leq-0004.analysis: Economics led: the voyages were organized around trade and wealth. Religion and rivalry shaped the form: the Reconquista gave Spain crusading habits and conversion as a stated mission, and rivalry between crowns turned trade routes into a race. The causes worked together, with economics first.
apush-leq-0004.context: The search for Asian trade after Constantinople fell in 1453 made overland routes costly; the Reconquista ended at Granada in January 1492; Portugal had spent decades building an African sea route to Asia.
evidence: Demand for Asian spices and silks drove Portugal down the African coast; da Gama reached India by sea in 1498.
Spain, with no route of its own, funded Columbus west in 1492, and the Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided the new lands between the two crowns.
St. Augustine was founded in 1565 as a military guard post protecting the shipping lanes that carried Spanish silver home.
England used a joint-stock company under the First Charter of Virginia (1606) to spread the cost and risk of a colony among many investors.
apush-leq-0004.thesis: Economic motives were the main cause of European exploration of the Americas from 1492 to 1607: the search for Asian trade and wealth drove the voyages, though religion and rivalry shaped where and how exploration happened.

method: Blind solves recorded from the blind files only, before opening any question file. Lesson read end to end as a student first.

apush-saq-0009.a: One economic motive was the demand for Asian spices and silks. Europeans wanted these goods but could reach them only through costly overland routes, which grew more costly after Constantinople fell in 1453.
apush-saq-0009.b: The caravel's lateen sails let ships sail against the wind, so Portuguese crews could work their way down the African coast and back home again. Without a ship that could sail into the wind, the long coastal voyages would have been impossible.
apush-saq-0009.c: The search turned trade into a race between crowns, as Portugal built its African route and Spain funded Columbus to find a western one. Rivalry over routes, not only over land, became a cause of conflict between European powers.

apush-saq-0010.a: Columbus claims the peoples he met were gentle, timid, and well built, had no iron weapons, and gave freely what they had. He presents them as unarmed and welcoming.
apush-saq-0010.b: Columbus wrote to report his voyage to the Spanish monarchs and to persuade them that the lands were worth further voyages. His glowing account of fertile land and gold served that purpose, since it promised profit from more expeditions.
apush-saq-0010.c: His reports of gold and gentle peoples encouraged Spain to fund more voyages and to claim the lands. The picture he painted of unarmed, welcoming peoples also helped justify conquest, since it suggested the lands could be taken cheaply.

apush-saq-0011.a: The painting shows Columbus standing at the center of the landing party, holding a Spanish flag while armed men stand around him. Indigenous people watch from the trees at the right of the scene, with ships at anchor behind.
apush-saq-0011.b: The painting places Columbus at the center as a heroic figure carrying the flag, which shows that 19th-century viewers celebrated him as a founder of the Americas. The image honors the landing rather than questioning it, so it tells us about 1862 as much as about 1492.
apush-saq-0011.c: The painting was made in 1862, nearly four centuries after the landing, by an artist who was not there. It shows what a 19th-century painter imagined, not what the shore looked like in 1492.

apush-saq-0012.a: One term of the treaty was that the dividing line was moved 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde islands. The new line gave Portugal Brazil and kept Spain's claim to the rest of the Americas.
apush-saq-0012.b: Both crowns were Catholic and still recognized the pope as an authority who could settle disputes between Catholic rulers, so they accepted his role in dividing the lands.
apush-saq-0012.c: One consequence for Portugal was that it secured Brazil, and the line protected its African sea route to Asia.

apush-saq-0013.a: Hakluyt argues England should plant colonies to find a route to Asia, to provide work for England's idle poor, and to spread Protestant Christianity.
apush-saq-0013.b: Hakluyt warned that Spain was growing rich from the Americas and that England must act before Spain took everything, so his argument is driven by rivalry with Spain.
apush-saq-0013.c: England was slow because of religious turmoil at home and a costly war with Spain, which kept it out until the defeat of the Spanish Armada in 1588; Roanoke then failed in 1587 and no lasting colony came until Jamestown in 1607.
